us-pcac-2026-peptide-vote.title: US advisers back six peptides for pharmacy compounding
us-pcac-2026-peptide-vote.summary: On 23 July 2026 the FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to recommend BPC-157 for the 503A list of ingredients pharmacies may use. Over two days it considered seven peptides and recommended six: BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax and epitalon, but not emideltide. These results are as reported from the public meeting; the FDA has posted no minutes. The vote is advice only, and went against FDA staff's own proposal. Compounding with these peptides stays prohibited until the FDA adopts the advice and completes rulemaking. None of them is an approved medicine in the US, the UK, Canada or Australia (Semax is registered as a medicine in Russia). A listing would let US pharmacies compound them on prescription. It would not be an approval, would say nothing about whether they work, and would change nothing outside the US.
us-pcac-2026-peptide-vote.next: The FDA decides whether to propose a rule, which would then be open for public comment. No date has been set. On 23 October 2026 the Federal Register held no proposed rule.

us-pcac-2027-meeting.title: A second FDA advisory meeting on five more substances
us-pcac-2027-meeting.summary: The FDA says it will hold another advisory meeting before the end of February 2027. It will discuss LL-37, GHK-Cu, dihexa acetate, melanotan II and pegylated mechano growth factor (PEG-MGF) for the 503A list. The date and place are not yet set.
us-pcac-2027-meeting.next: A Federal Register notice with the date and a public docket, then the meeting before the end of February 2027

us-503a-interim-categories.title: FDA compounding categories: peptide nominations withdrawn, none in category 1
us-503a-interim-categories.summary: While it builds the 503A list, the FDA sorts nominated ingredients into three interim categories. By 22 April 2026 it listed BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, CJC-1295, AOD-9604, Semax, epitalon and other peptides as 'previously in category 2', because their nominations were withdrawn. Its list of 14 May 2026 puts none of them in category 1, the only category for which the FDA says it does not intend to act against pharmacies. The one exception is GHK-Cu for routes other than injection. The FDA no longer sorts ingredients nominated since 7 January 2025 into these categories.
us-503a-interim-categories.next: Any change appears in an updated FDA list of categories

us-503b-glp1-exclusion.title: FDA proposes to keep semaglutide and tirzepatide off the 503B list
us-503b-glp1-exclusion.summary: On 30 April 2026 the FDA proposed not to put semaglutide, tirzepatide or liraglutide on the list of bulk ingredients that outsourcing facilities may use, because it found no clinical need. Comments closed on 30 July 2026. The shortages that allowed wider compounding ended earlier: for tirzepatide on 19 December 2024, for semaglutide on 21 February 2025.
us-503b-glp1-exclusion.next: The FDA's final decision, to be published in the Federal Register. No date has been set; on 23 October 2026 none had been published.

us-ruo-warning-letters.title: FDA warning letters to 'research use only' peptide sellers
us-ruo-warning-letters.summary: The FDA keeps sending warning letters to online sellers of peptides labelled 'research use only'. Letters of March and August 2026 say the sellers' own websites show the products are drugs for people, so they are unapproved new drugs. Bacteriostatic water sold with them counts as a drug too. The FDA warns that such products are of unknown quality.
us-ruo-warning-letters.next: New letters appear in the FDA's warning letter database

eu-pharma-reform.title: The EU's new medicines law
eu-pharma-reform.summary: The EU is replacing its main medicines law, Directive 2001/83/EC, with a new directive and a new regulation. Parliament and Council reached political agreement on 11 December 2025. The Council published its position on 1 October 2026, and both texts now wait for Parliament's second reading. After the new law enters into force, member states get a transition period to update their own laws; the EMA expects it to run until 2028. Until then, today's rules apply.
eu-pharma-reform.next: Parliament's plenary vote; the European Parliament gives 23 November 2026 as an indicative date

wada-2027-prohibited-list.title: The 2027 Prohibited List names peptides in section S0
wada-2027-prohibited-list.summary: WADA published the 2027 Prohibited List on 21 September 2026. It takes effect on 1 January 2027. Section S0 now names 'peptides' among its examples, next to BPC-157. WADA says a peptide that the list does not name may still be prohibited. UK Anti-Doping adds that not every banned experimental peptide is named on the list.

wada-2027-code.title: A new World Anti-Doping Code from 1 January 2027
wada-2027-code.summary: WADA approved the 2027 World Anti-Doping Code and its standards on 5 December 2025, including a new standard for medical exemptions (TUEs). Both take effect on 1 January 2027. Strict liability stays: a banned substance in your sample is a violation, whatever you intended.
wada-2027-code.next: The 2027 Code and standards take effect

wada-glp1-monitoring.title: Semaglutide and tirzepatide stay on WADA's watch list
wada-glp1-monitoring.summary: Semaglutide and tirzepatide are not banned in sport. WADA keeps them in its 2027 Monitoring Program, in and out of competition, to see whether athletes misuse them. They were also in the 2026 programme.
wada-glp1-monitoring.next: WADA's next yearly Prohibited List and Monitoring Program

uk-mhra-weight-loss-raids.title: MHRA raids on unlicensed weight-loss injections
uk-mhra-weight-loss-raids.summary: Since October 2025 the UK medicines regulator has raided several sites that made unlicensed retatrutide and tirzepatide pens, including a farm in Lincolnshire in February 2026 and a property near Northampton in May 2026. On 14 October 2026 it seized more than 12,000 fake pens in Birmingham. The MHRA says products sold as retatrutide outside clinical trials are supplied illegally.

de-doping-list-gazette.title: Germany's doping law follows the WADA list each year
de-doping-list-gazette.summary: Germany's anti-doping law bans selling and supplying substances on the WADA list, as published each year in the federal law gazette. The 2026 list appeared there on 23 December 2025. A separate annex of the law, last changed in March 2023, decides which substances are a crime to own in large amounts. It names TB-500 and several growth-hormone peptides, but not BPC-157.
de-doping-list-gazette.next: Publication of the 2027 list in the federal law gazette

nl-igj-online-sellers.title: Dutch inspectorate: more reports about illegal online medicine sellers
nl-igj-online-sellers.summary: The Dutch Health and Youth Care Inspectorate (IGJ) received 114 reports in 2024 about web shops selling prescription medicines without a prescription, and 187 from January to early October 2025. It investigated 150 sites and had dozens taken down. The reports are not only about peptides. The IGJ can warn or fine websites that offer or advertise illegal medicines to Dutch buyers.

uk-high-risk-wellbeing-procedures.title: England: a plan to restrict "wellbeing" drips and other high-risk procedures
uk-high-risk-wellbeing-procedures.summary: The UK government is consulting on rules for high-risk cosmetic and wellbeing procedures in England. They include putting a substance into a vein for a cosmetic or wellbeing reason, such as a vitamin drip. Only doctors, dentists and some prescribing nurses, midwives and pharmacists could do them, not for under-18s except in NHS care or to treat a medical condition, and providers would have to register with the Care Quality Commission. Breaking the rules would be a crime. The plan does not name peptides or NAD+.
uk-high-risk-wellbeing-procedures.next: The consultation closes on 13 January 2027. A transition period would come before the rules apply

ca-hc-injectable-peptides-enforcement.title: Canada: Health Canada acts against unauthorised injectable peptides
ca-hc-injectable-peptides-enforcement.summary: In April 2026 Health Canada warned the public about injectable peptides sold online, among them BPC-157, CJC-1295, TB-500 and retatrutide. It said these products are illegal and unassessed, that a 'research use only' label does not make them legal, and that it works with the border agency to stop shipments. Alberta's regulator of doctors warned its members the same month. In May 2026 Health Canada recalled BPC-157 and GHK-Cu powder that had been sold to pharmacies as unauthorised ingredients. None of the 2026 changes to Canada's list of prescription drugs concerns these peptides.
ca-hc-injectable-peptides-enforcement.next: Further Health Canada advisories and recalls

au-personal-import-packaging.title: Australia: new rules for medicines you import for yourself
au-personal-import-packaging.summary: Since 8 September 2026, a medicine you import for yourself under the Personal Importation Scheme must be in packaging that identifies it; the TGA asks that it stays in its original packaging where possible. Travellers who bring in a prescription-only medicine now also need a written authority from a doctor. Goods that do not meet the rules may be seized, and the money paid is lost. The same regulations make clear that medicines made up by a pharmacy for one person may not be advertised to the public.

au-tga-peptide-compliance-priority.title: Australia: unapproved peptides are a TGA enforcement priority
au-tga-peptide-compliance-priority.summary: In June 2026 the TGA added unapproved peptide products to its compliance priorities, after more unlawful importing, supply and advertising. With the Chief Medical Officer it warned of liver damage, severe allergic reactions and inflammation linked to unapproved peptides. On 28 September 2026 it started Federal Court proceedings against a former company and its directors over the advertising of peptides such as BPC-157 and CJC-1295. On 6 October 2026 it announced infringement notices, including to people who imported prescription-only medicines without approval.
au-tga-peptide-compliance-priority.next: Further TGA enforcement news; no hearing date for the court case has been published

au-nsw-medicines-law-2026.title: Australia (New South Wales): new medicines and poisons laws from 5 November 2026
au-nsw-medicines-law-2026.summary: From 5 November 2026, the Medicines, Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act 2022 and a new 2026 Regulation replace the state's 1966 poisons law and its Regulation. Schedule 4D medicines are prescription medicines with stricter rules on who may have them: under the new law too, NSW Health says, only a person to whom one was lawfully prescribed or supplied, or their carer, may have it. A prescription for one will be valid for 12 months instead of 6. NSW Health's list of these medicines under the new Regulation names TB-500, CJC-1295, ipamorelin, hexarelin and AOD-9604, but not BPC-157 or melanotan II. We have not read the new Regulation, or the Act as it starts.
au-nsw-medicines-law-2026.next: The new laws start on 5 November 2026

au-advertising-code-review.title: Australia: a review of the code for advertising medicines
au-advertising-code-review.summary: The TGA asked for comments on ways to improve the Therapeutic Goods Advertising Code, which sets the standards for advertising medicines and other health products to the public. Comments closed on 3 September 2026. The TGA will publish its decisions on the consultation page; none had appeared by 24 October 2026. The review is not about peptides only.
au-advertising-code-review.next: The TGA's decisions, to be published on the consultation page
